IN RE: DAVID KAUFMAN
PETITION FOR Review for Personal Income Tax
PERIOD(S) 2011
AND NOW, May 20, 2014, pursuant to the Fiscal Code, the Act of 1929, April 9, P.L. 343,
as amended, (72 P.S. § 1 et seq), the Board of Finance and Revenue of the Commonwealth of
Pennsylvania, based upon the reasons set forth herein, hereby ORDERS the following:
Jurisdiction
This petition comes before the Board of Finance and Revenue pursuant to Section 2704
of the Tax Reform Code of 1971, as amended, 72 P.S. § 9704.
Issue
Whether Petitioner has established that he was domiciled in and a resident of Florida
during the 2011 tax year.
Statement of the Case
Petitioner, David Kaufman, and his spouse, Mary A. Kaufman, filed a 2011 Form PA-40
as non-residents and reporting no taxable income. Petitioners reported their address as
.
The Department of Revenue determined that Petitioner and his spouse were residents
of the Commonwealth because, among other things, they received certain tax documents at a
Pennsylvania address; owned a Pennsylvania residence; received a homestead exemption on
the Pennsylvania residence; registered multiple vehicles in Pennsylvania; and Petitioner’s
spouse received two Schedules RK-1 from entities located in Pennsylvania. The Department
issued an assessment notice in the amount of $ , including tax, penalties, and
interest.

Petitioner protested the assessment notice at the Board of Appeals (”BOA”) claiming
that he and his spouse were domiciled in Florida as of March 10, 2010, and, as such, were no
longer resident individuals of the Commonwealth. By letter and e-mail dated October 18,
2013, the BOA requested that Petitioner’s representative submit a properly completed power
of attorney form in order to perfect the appeal. The correspondence requested that Petitioner’s
representative provide the form within 15 days of the date of the correspondence. By Decision
and Order dated December 19, 2013, the BOA denied Petitioner’s appeal for failure to provide
the power of attorney form.
Petitioner files the instant matter at the Board of Finance and Revenue protesting the
BOA’s Decision and Order. In the appeal filed with this Board, Petitioner’s representative
states that he provided the BOA with documentation to support Petitioner’s claim that he and
his spouse were not domiciled in Pennsylvania during 2010, including legal principals,
arguments, and eight exhibits.
In the appeal filed at the BOA, Petitioner claimed that Florida was his state of domicile
during 2011, because he and his spouse established Florida as their domicile and base of
operations beginning in March 2010. Petitioner stated that a taxpayer's domicile is the state in
which the taxpayer maintains his or her permanent place of abode, and is the place where he
or she intends to return whenever absent. Further, Petitioner stated that when a taxpayer
maintains multiple “permanent abodes,” his domicile is the place where the taxpayer has the
greatest connections and the place which the taxpayer intends to be his or her domicile.
Petitioner stated that an abode is not permanent if it is occupied “only during a fixed or limited
period of time for a particular purpose.” Petitioner asserted that when determining domicile,
the Department was required to consider where the taxpayer spends the greatest amount of
his or her time, where the taxpayer purchases the necessities of life, maintains expensive
furniture or works of art, maintains a driver's license, registers vehicles, maintains hunting or
fishing licenses, carries insurance policies, registers to vote, and files federal income tax
returns.
Petitioner argued that he and his spouse purchased their home in Florida in March
2010, at which time, they transported family photos, works of art, and the necessities of daily
life to the Florida home. Petitioner also contended that they transferred vehicle registrations to
Florida, obtained Florida driver's licenses, registered to vote in Florida, participated in elections
in Florida, and served on jury duty in Florida. Petitioner states that he and his spouse revoked
their will executed in Pennsylvania in favor of a will executed in Florida. Further, Petitioner
states that he and his spouse have only been present in Pennsylvania for limited periods of
time in order to visit family members who still reside in the state. Petitioner contends that he
and his spouse have been domiciled in Florida since March 2010, and are therefore exempted
from Pennsylvania personal income taxes for all subsequent years.
To support the appeal, Petitioner has submitted the following:
• A spreadsheet reporting the number of days that Petitioner claims to have spent in
different states during 2011. The spreadsheet reports that Petitioner spent 143 days in
Pennsylvania, 129 days in Florida, 53 days in Maryland, and 40 days in Nevada during
2011.

• A declaration page for a homeowners’ insurance policy on Petitioner’s Florida home.

Statement of the Law
Every resident individual, estate or trust shall be subject to, and shall pay for the
privilege of receiving each of the classes of income hereinafter enumerated in section 303, a
tax upon each dollar of income received by that resident during that resident's taxable year at
the rate of three and seven hundredths per cent. 72 P.S. § 7302(a).
“Resident Individual” means an individual who is domiciled in this Commonwealth
unless he maintains no permanent place of abode in this Commonwealth and does maintain a
permanent place of abode elsewhere and spends in the aggregate not more than thirty days of
the taxable year in this Commonwealth; or who is not domiciled in this Commonwealth but
maintains a permanent place of the abode in this Commonwealth and spends in the aggregate
more than one hundred eighty-three days of taxable year in this Commonwealth.
72 P.S. § 7301(p).
Domicile—The place which an individual intends to be his permanent home and to
which he intends to return whenever he may be absent. 61 Pa. Code § 101.1.
A domicile, once established, continues until the individual in question moves to a new
location with the bona fide intention of making his fixed and permanent home there. No
change of domicile results from a removal to a new location if the intention is to remain there
only for a limited time; this rule applies even though the individual may have sold or disposed
of his former home. The burden shall be upon the individual asserting a change of domicile to
show that the necessary intention exited. In determining an individual’s intention in this regard,
his declarations shall be given due weight, but they may not be conclusive if they are
contradicted by his conduct. The fact that an individual registers and votes in one place is
important but not necessarily conclusive, especially if the facts indicate that he did this merely
to escape taxation in some other place. 61 Pa. Code § 101.3(b).

Where an individual claims to be a nonresident for any taxable year, the burden shall be
upon him to show that during that he satisfied all there of the requirements set forth in
subsection (a). 61 Pa. Code § 101.4(b).
“Homestead.” A dwelling, including the parcel of land on which the dwelling is located
and the other improvements located on the parcel for which any of the following apply:
(1) The dwelling is primarily used as the domicile of an owner who is a natural person.
The homestead for real property qualifying under this paragraph shall not include the
land on which the dwelling is located if the land is not owned by a person who owns the
dwelling.
(2) The dwelling is a unit in a condominium as the term is defined in 68 Pa.C.S. § 3103
(relating to definitions) and the unit is primarily used as the domicile of a natural person
who is an owner of the unit; or the dwelling is a unit in a cooperative as the term is
defined in 68 Pa.C.S. § 4103 (relating to definitions) and the unit is primarily used as the
domicile of a natural person who is an owner of the unit. The homestead for a unit in a
condominium or a cooperative shall be limited to the assessed value of the unit, which
shall be determined in a manner consistent with the assessment of real property taxes
on those units under 68 Pa.C.S. (relating to real and personal property) or as otherwise
provided by law. If the unit is not separately assessed for real property taxes, the
homestead shall be a pro rata share of the real property.
(3) The dwelling does not qualify under paragraphs (1) and (2) and a portion of the
dwelling is used as the domicile of an owner who is a natural person. The homestead
for real property qualifying under this paragraph shall be the portion of the real property
that is equal to the portion of the dwelling that is used as the domicile of an owner.
53 Pa.C.S.A. § 8401 “Homestead.”
Upon the filing of a petition for reassessment or a petition for refund as provided under
this act by a taxpayer, additions or penalties imposed upon the taxpayer by the laws of this
Commonwealth may be waived or abated, in whole or in part, where the petitioner has
established that he has acted in good faith, without negligence and with no intent to defraud.
72 P.S. § 9706.
Except as otherwise provided by this act, in all cases of petitions filed pursuant to this
article, the burden of proof shall be upon the petitioner or appellant, as the case may be.
72 P.S. § 9705.
Conclusion
Petitioner’s request that this Board determine that he was not a resident individual for
tax purposes is denied because, among other reasons, he maintained a homestead exemption
in the Commonwealth and spent more time in Pennsylvania during 2011 than any other state.
A homestead exemption is only available to a Pennsylvania resident and for that resident’s
permanent primary residence on which property taxes are paid. See 53 Pa.C.S.A. § 8401

“Homestead.” (defining “homestead,” in part, as a dwelling “primarily used as the domicile of
an owner who is a natural person”).
Resident taxpayers are required to pay personal income tax to the Commonwealth for
the privilege of receiving eight enumerated classes of income. See 72 P.S. § 7302(a)
(imposing personal income tax on residents). The term “resident individual” is defined, in part,
as “an individual who is domiciled in this Commonwealth unless he maintains no permanent
place of abode in this Commonwealth and does maintain a permanent place of abode
elsewhere and spends in the aggregate not more than thirty days of the taxable year in this
Commonwealth.” 72 P.S. § 7301(p). The term “domicile” is defined as “[t]he place which an
individual intends to be his permanent home and to which he intends to return whenever he
may be absent.” 61 Pa. Code § 101.1. Domicile continues until the taxpayer moves to new
location with the bona fide intention of making a fixed and permanent home there. 61 Pa.
Code § 101.3(b). In Hvizdak v. Commonwealth, the Commonwealth Court stated that the
Pennsylvania “Supreme Court stated that ‘a domicile of choice may not be retained by
intention alone.’ It must also be shown by one's conduct.” 50 A.3d 788 (Pa Commw. 2012)
(citing Dorrance's Estate, 309 Pa. 151, 170, 163 A. 303, 309 (1932)), aff’d, 69 A.3d 170 (Pa.
2013).
The Board has determined that Petitioner has not met his burden of establishing that he
relinquished his Pennsylvania residency. Additionally, Petitioner spent the greatest portion of
2011 in the Commonwealth, 143 days of 365 days, further showing that he did not change his
domicile to Florida.
Accordingly, the Board orders the following:
ORDER
This petition is denied.
